If Canada were a desert or semi-desert there might be some excuse for dealing with them in this fashion. But our country is capable of producing not only abundance but superabundance. I say that in dealing with these people the attitude constantly adopted is to beat down their just desserts and to give them just as little as can be got away with. What we ought to do is to err on the side of generosity, rather than the reverse.
Another point in connection with pensions is this: I believe every aged person, not at seventy years but at least at sixty-five should receive his pension automatically, whether he be rich or poor, and without any application. That is part of the cultural and national heritage to which the aged are entitled, simply by reason of their citizenship in this wonderful country. I say, therefore, that although there has been much equalization of income, there are still many in the lower brackets whose incomes should be raised, before we can say there is the greatest possible equality of sacrifice. Just so long as that position obtains, I believe our war effort will be impaired.
There are many of the older generation, registered as unemployables, who would like to contribute each day an hour or a couple of hours of work of some kind, in order to make their contribution to the war effort. But on account of their meagre incomes they are unable to do so. They cannot avail themselves of the necessary health services, with the result that we are losing that much energy which could be directed toward our war effort if those incomes were raised to what they ought to be.
I have some further criticisms respecting the budget, and I believe these apply to a peace-time budget equally as well as to one
brought down in war time. I contend that a budget proper should set forth in financial terms all that has taken place in physical terms. This budget does not do so. A budget proper should be a complete financial reflection of the physical realities of the nation. This budget is not such. A budget proper should not represent the creation of new and additional real wealth as a national liability. This budget does so. A budget proper should represent the production of all new real wealth as a national asset. This budget does not do so. A budget proper should not indicate that a nation is headed for financial bankruptcy, when it has greater real wealth producing powers than ever before in its history. This budget does so.
Both the Minister of Finance and the deputy minister have asserted that the real costs of the war are the men and materials, and that such costs must be borne by the generation fighting the war. I agree entirely with that position. But the point I make is that the minister's confession of faith, and his works, do not harmonize. The budget brought down by the minister is not a reflection of the real facts in his possession. In physical terms the armed forces and workers in munitions factories, the miners, lumbermen, fishermen and bank clerks, and all others, have met all the real costs of the war. On the other hand, the budget is not a reflection of that fact.
When we examine the budget we see that our national debt is to be increased to the extent of about two and a quarter billion dollars. That increase in national debt suggests that the people of Canada are not paying for the war as it is being fought. Speaking in Montreal, as recorded by the Financial Post, the deputy minister of finance, Dr. Clark, made the statement that by no financial sleight-of-hand can we pass on the burden of war to oncoming generations. But is that not exactly what is being done in the budget? The point I make is that either the minister's statements are wrong, or the budget policy is wrong. They cannot both be right, because one is a contradiction of the other. If the minister's statements are correct, then the budget policy is wrong. My personal belief is that the minister's statements are correct, and that the budget policy is wrong.
I contend that war debt is a positively false situation. War debt in a country with the wealth producing power of Canada is pure fiction. Canada has no real war debt. The only reason why the budget indicates that the people of Canada have a war debt arises

The Budget-Mr. Kuhl
from the fact that the government is pursuing an upside-down financial policy. It is a policy which conceals, rather than reveals facts.
I should! like to make some remarks respecting the manner in which bond sales campaigns are conducted. I have several objections to the manner in which these sales are made. I was both shocked and amazed when I heard a statement made by those speaking on behalf of tire workers who took part in the last victory loan campaign. I did not imagine that any responsible individual could make a statement so far from the truth. This is the question I heard asked over the air, one for which I have no doubt the war finance committee is responsible: "How would you like to fight Hitler without leaving your comfortable fireside?" I contend that a statement of that kind is not only false but actually subversive of the war effort. It fosters a false psychology in the minds of our people. It suggests that the purchaser of a bond1 is making a contribution almost equivalent to that made by the soldier, the sailor or the airman in the thick of the fight. It suggests that the purchaser of a bond is rendering a service equivalent to that of the individual who machines a gun barrel. I I object strenuously to that type of propaganda. The only way in which anyone can fight Hitler is by donning battle dress, shouldering a gun and participating in the actual conflict. To suggest that the purchaser of a gilt-edged revenue-bearing asset is making a sacrifice comparable with that of a soldier, sailor or airman is to be guilty of the basest blasphemy.
Another objection I take to the manner in which these campaigns are handled and the things that are said is that the people are led by the propaganda to believe that the government needs this money for the purchase of guns, planes, tanks and ships and other war material. In fact they are led to believe that the actual money produces the weapons. I have here a page from the Financial Post which bears out that point. This is an advertisement which came out during the last victory loan campaign. It says:
What our $750 millions will do.
Build 2,208 ram tanks for the army.
Build 55 corvettes for the navy.
Build 397 Lancasters for Britain.
I say that is giving an entirely false impression of the objects of a loan campaign. The minister has stated again and again that the object of the sale of bonds, war savings certificates and stamps is not primarily to raise money to buy ships and tanks and guns and munitions; that its major purpose, if not
its only purpose, is to curtail civilian spending, to reduce the pressure on the purchase of civilian goods in order that more materials may be directed toward the war. If that is the true position; if that is the real object of the sale of bonds, I suggest to the Minister of Finance that he see to it that no other impression goes abroad among our people.
Another point I should like to make-it has been made already in previous debates by one of my colleagues-is with regard to paying interest on bonds, war savings certificates and stamps. If the primary, if not the only purpose of the sale of these bonds and certificates is to curtail civilian spending, then this money which is involved in their purchase constitutes savings. And I believe that if the people are to be permitted to make savings out of their war earnings they should do so at their own expense. Instead of the government paying the people interest on their savings, the people should be obliged to pay the government a service charge for handling their accounts for them during the war. The -reason why the people expect interest on their bonds and savings certificates is that they have been led to believe that the government needs their money to buy tanks and guns and ships, whereas the fact is that as far as securing the money is concerned, if the government chose and wished to do so, the government could create in one minute sufficient money to run this war for the next hundred years. The extent of the money the government created would be simply a matter of the number of naughts they added to the first digit on the credit side of the ledger. In saying that, I am not implying that ships and tanks and guns can be manufactured overnight, but certainly the procuring of the money is the simplest thing in the world; it is nothing but bookkeeping entries.
Another point I should like to make in regard to taking money from the people in order to curtail civilian spending is that the present method through the sale of bonds, war savings certificates and stamps is extremely wasteful of materials and energy, if the primary purpose is to deprive the people temporarily of their spending power. The printing of those bonds involves skilled workmanship and high-class paper. That work and material is absolutely unnecessary. During these bond campaigns salesmen by the hundreds are spending their time urging the people to invest. This labour could be saved; these people could be far better employed behind a lathe machining gun barrels or something of that kind. That would constitute a real contribution. The same thing applies to
The Budget-Mr. Kuhl

advertising; the tremendous radio and newspaper and other advertising programmes are a waste of time, energy and material.
Another objection I have to the present policy is that because all people are unable to purchase bonds and certificates to the extent they would like, it places the majority of the people of Canada in pawn to about fifteen per cent of the people of Canada. The majority become bond-slaves forever to the few.
So much for my criticisms as to the present methods of taking from the people their surplus purchasing power. Let me now say a few words in connection with the sale of bonds to the chartered banks for the purpose of obtaining money. The objectionable features of the present method of handling bonds are bad enough, but those with regard to bank borrowings are infinitely worse. I would not object so seriously if the banks bought these bonds out of their earnings, but they do not. The $790,000,000 of bonds that were purchased by the chartered banks during the last financial year were purchased with money which they themselves created for themselves at no cost to themselves and without assuming any responsibility. The money which the government raised from the chartered banks to the extent of $790,000,000 last year was brand new money. It was purely bookkeeping entries, but brand new money nevertheless, additional to what was already in existence. My contention i3 that the right and privilege of creating this money is a crown prerogative; it is the highest prerogative that the crown can enjoy, namely, creating the money of the nation. But as a result of government policy, $790,000,000 at least was created last year by private institutions, and the people as a whole placed in pawn to the banking institutions. Mr. Barclay Smith, an Australian writer, in a book entitled "Victory Without Debt" has this to say on that point:
It is infamous beyond words that private banks should have the power to make profits in perpetuity out of creating credit, when the government has full power to create its own monetary requirements without borrowing and taxing.
At six o'clock the house took recess.
After Recess
The house resumed at eight o'clock.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to associate myself with the remarks of the hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson) this afternoon with regard to the coming victory loan; and I wish to assure the Minister of Finance
(Mr. Ilsley) that as far as the section of Ontario from which I come is concerned, as in all other campaigns it will raise its share of the loan, just as already it has contributed its share during the current campaign for funds for the Red Cross.
In the debate on Tuesday concerning the fuel situation a great deal was said about the question of man-power, and I should like to bring to the attention of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) a matter in that connection which seriously affects eastern Ontario. I wish to quote from an article appearing in the Belleville Intelligencer of March 10, under the heading "Government officials to meet Ontario cheese men in city to discuss present shortage of factory help":
Of 342 cheese factories in Ontario which replied to questionnaires sent out by the eastern, central and western Ontario cheese makers' associations within the past few days, 257 reported that they rvere in need of immediate help if the requested 1943 increased cheese production is to be achieved. ... At a recent meeting, officials of the three associations endorsed a resolution recommending the sending of an official delegation to Ottawa to seek immediate alleviation of the labour problem. ... In all, it was stated, the factories required 309 experienced men immediately if operations, which usually start between April 15 and May 1, are to get away on time.
Belleville is the centre of the cheese industry in eastern Ontario.
Last session I brought to the attention of the then Minister of National War Services, whose department at that time was administering the call up of men for the armed forces, the seriousness of the situation resulting from calling up experienced cheese makers and helpers for military service, but apparently nothing was done, since the divisional registrars continued to call up these men. Only a short time ago a cheese maker in my county came to me in regard to two of his experienced helpers who had been called up for training. With the time approaching for the opening of his factory, which would produce from 150,000 to 175,000 pounds of cheese per annum, he was confronted with the situation that he had no help. As everyone knows, the farmers have been requested to increase to a great extent their cheese production during 1943, and the average farmer has made provision to do so. It seems most unfortunate that at this time of year, when the factories are ready to open, we should find a most serious shortage of these skilled men, and I sincerely trust that the delegation which is to see the minister will be able to discover some way to remedy this situation.

The Budget-Mr. White
In a return brought down in this house on March 15 last, sessional paper No. 139B, there are set out the enlistments in the armed forces up to January 31, 1943. An examination of this report shows clearly the farce of the term "equality of service and sacrifice" as applied across Canada. I should like to place on Hansard the figures showing by military' districts the male population between the ages of nineteen and forty-five, and the number of enlistments:
		Male population 19-45	Enlistments
MiD.	1-London ....	147,800	32,649M.D.	2-Toronto ....	408,700	95,596M.D.	3-Kingston ...	150,000	42,144M.D.	4-Montreal .. .	423,800	50,654M.D.	5-Quebec 	214,300	17,403M.D.	6-Halifax ....	118,200	35,226M.D.	7-Saint John.	80,300	23,220M.D.	10-Winnipeg . .	179,700	37,326M.D.	11-Victoria ....	155,100	35,855M.D.	12-Regina 	177,200	31,602M.D.	13-Calgary ....	160,700	34,983 436,658
An examination of this return will clearly show that there is no equality of service spread evenly across Canada, and will show the heavy load some districts are bearing in comparison with others as far as voluntary enlistments are concerned. In the last issue of "Canada at War", at page 39 under the heading of "man-power" I note the following statement:
Approximately 33 per cent of all male Canadians between the ages of 19 and 45 have enlisted in the armed services.
How much better it would have been to point out that in eight provinces of Canada the enlistments were well over thirty-three per cent, but that in Quebec, the ninth province, they ran somewhere between ten and fifteen per cent. In my opinion this condition can be corrected only by the introduction of a fair and just system of selective military service applied in the same manner and degree to all parts of Canada. On other occasions I have advocated the same policy in the house. I did so as far back as June, 1940. At that time one was almost guilty of treason or liable to be charged under the defence of Canada regulations if he made such a suggestion. Then, as now, it was claimed that the introduction of such a system would destroy national unity, but I for one could never understand why a fair and proper distribution of man-power to be called up for military service across the whole dominion should interfere with or destroy our national unity. The National Resources Mobilization
Act has been a farce from the start. On February 26, 1943, replying to a question asked in the house, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) stated that he had not changed his mind in any way about the amendment to this act passed at the last session, and that before the act could be put into force it would be necessary to come back to this house for a vote of confidence or want of confidence in the government. What a man-power policy to have in the fourth year of the war! What a farce the plebiscite turned out to be. With the zero hour for the invasion of Europe drawing closer every day, we have not as yet adopted a proper man-power policy.
With regard to the matter of reinforcements for our forces overseas I think all members of the house will await with interest the secret session at which I trust the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) will take us all into his confidence and tell us quite frankly the whole story of our reinforcements for overseas. Dieppe showed casualties of some sixty-seven per cent of those taking part, so that it will be most interesting to hear from the Minister of National Defence the details of the provisions that have been made for providing reinforcements for our troops now in Great Britain.
Yesterday the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) showed that the army was not receiving the proper number of reinforcements month by month. He based his remarks upon the official return No. 139B, which I now hold in my hand, and other figures contained in the booklet "Canada at War". The Minister of National Defence disputed the correctness of his figures, but he gave no explanation as to how the mistakes had occurred. I should like to point out to the Minister of National Defence that the error mentioned yesterday by the hon. member for Lake Centre is not the only one.
If hon. members will look at page 14 of the January issue of "Canada at War", they will see under the heading "army" that the number of soldiers in the active army in Canada is given as 210,000. Yet this return shows the total number of men by military districts, attested for service anywhere but now serving in Canada, as 149,000 as of January 2, 1943. This is a mere difference of 61,000 men. On the same page of the January issue of "Canada at War" the number of men in the reserve army is shown as 200,000; yet in this return it is stated that the total number of men by military districts who were serving with the reserve army as of December 31, 1942, is
The Budget-Mr. White

106,000. This is another slight difference of only 94,000 men. I assume that in the figure of 106,000, being the total number of men serving in the reserve army, is included the
60.000	to 70,000 men who received training for only one month.
The March issue of "Canada at War", which is just off the press, gives on page 14 the strength of the active army as 430,000; yet yesterday the Minister of National Defence pointed out that, according to the return brought down the strength of the army was 437,203; he gave the enlistments for January, 1943, as 11,631, and for February, 8,927, making a total of 457,761. This is another small difference of 27,761.
I do not suggest that the figures given by the minister are wrong, but it seems peculiar that when the ordinary private member is able to obtain information only from returns such as this and from official government publications such as "Canada at War", he should find these great discrepancies. "Canada at War" is issued by the wartime information board, a department of this government. It is only fair to assume that these officials have access to proper sources of information. Perhaps "Canada at War" is issued only for political propaganda purposes; I do not know. This return shows that up to January 31 of this year the number of men called up under the National Resources Mobilization Act was 114,641. I think I am quite safe in saying that to secure this number of men, at least
900.000	notices would have to be sent out.
An examination of the table of enlistments
on page 22 of the February issue of "Canada at War" shows that the call up of men under the National Resources Mobilization Act is not carried out on a proper percentage basis according to population. Let me take military district No. 1 at London as an example. This district has a population of 147,800, and it has supplied by voluntary enlistments a total of 32,378 men for the army. From this district there were called up under the National Resources Mobilization Act a total of 8,533. Compare these figures with those of military district No. 5 at Quebec, with a male population of 214,300. The increase in population over the other district is 66,500. Military district No. 5 at Quebec supplied 17,492 men for the army, which is considerably less than half the number supplied by military district No. 1 at London. Military district No. 5 has supplied only 8,874 men under the National Resources Mobilization Act. These figures can be compared with those of other districts and the same condition will be found to exist.

I realize that the Minister of National Defence is not responsible in any way for the calling up of these men, but I think the time has come when the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) should tell this house and the public of Canada the plan or the scheme or the method used in his department in calling up men under the National Resources Mobilization Act. When the appropriation bill was before the house at the last session I attempted to secure from the then Minister of National War Services information as to what plan he operated under, but all that he could say was that the calling up of these men was fairly administered. I submit that the proper answer is to be found in this table put out by the government in the publication "Canada at War", in its February issue, which clearly shows that under the National Resources Mobilization Act far more men were called up from one district than were called up from another.
The time has come for the Minister of Labour to tell us exactly how if, say, 10,000 men are required to be called up in March under the National Resources Mobilization Act, they are allotted according to military districts across Canada. Does he consider calling up according to population, those between the ages of nineteen and forty-five? Does he consider the number of men who already have enlisted voluntarily from certain districts in the army, navy or air force? Or, what plan is it that he follows? I hope that either to-day or very soon the Minister of Labour will make a clear-cut statement to the house so that everybody will know what system is to be followed in the calling up of men under the National Resources Mobilization Act. I repeat, that only by the adoption of a fair and just system of national selective service under which men will be called up in a fair distribution across the whole of this dominion, irrespective of occupation, race, creed or anything else, can we cure the present situation. After all, why should one section of this country supply a far larger number of reinforcements than any other section? To-day eight provinces in Canada are more than doing their fair share, both in voluntary enlistments and in supplying men under the National Resources Mobilization Act. The province of Quebec is far behind the other provinces in the number of men who have enlisted voluntarily and in the number of men called up under the National Resources Mobilization Act. Yet there are men in this house who will talk day after day about equality of sacrifice and equality of service. But if anyone dares to suggest that Quebec lags behind, the old bogey of national unity is trotted out again.

The Budget-Mr. White
Why must the eight other provinces submerge their interests in favour of the province of Quebec?
Press releases show that under the National Resources Mobilization Act the draft dodgers run well into hundreds of thousands; yet, according to the press fewer than three or four hundred of them have been located and prosecuted. Under such a system, how can the people of this country who have sons overseas be expected to be satisfied with or have any confidence in such a half-hearted slipshod method of administering the law of Canada? The Minister of Justice (Mr. St. Laurent) has on various occasions been prompt and alert to act when there have been alleged contraventions of the defence of Canada regulations. Perhaps he might as well devote some of his time to administering in a proper, just and fair manner the regulations under the National Resources Mobilization Act.
A short time ago there appeared in the press of Canada an announcement that high-school students would again be allowed to leave school early in the summer term to engage in farm work and in industries connected with the war effort, and that any such student who worked for thirteen weeks would be granted his standing for the year, subject to the recommendation of his teacher or the principal of the school. I have no quarrel or complaint with that. But I .would point out that on March 8, the Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. Mackenzie) issued a statement in which he reviewed the educational qualifications of some 347,900 men in the armed forces. The statement showed that of that number the largest group, 102,892, were those in the junior matriculation class; those who had obtained their junior matriculation numbered 31,64S; and those having their senior matriculation, 1,120. But the strange thing is that young men in the province of Ontario who join the armed forces in their matriculation year are not granted their standing for that year. Surely some plan could be worked out with the provincial educational authorities whereby any boy in his matriculation year who joins the armed forces would be granted his educational standing for that year. Many hon. members will recall what happened at the end of the last war when the boys came home. Hundreds of them who had not obtained their junior or senior matriculation were prevented from going on and undertaking university or other courses.
In the estimates for the present year, under the Department of Pensions and National Health there is an item of $400,000 for pensions to be awarded to widows of deceased soldiers,
such pensions to be awarded on compassionate grounds. I would point out to the minister of pensions that while this is very commendable it merely touches the fringe of the whole question of pensions to widows of soldiers. As hon. members are aware, on the death of a soldier whose disability is fifty per cent or over, his widow continues to receive a pension. But on the death of a soldier having a disability of less than fifty per cent his widow receives no further pension. Take the case of a soldier with a wife, and receiving a monthly pension of $30 a month. Of that amount S20 is the pension awarded to the husband, and $10 is the amount payable because he is a married man. On the death of that soldier his wndow does not continue to receive the S10 that had been paid on her account; she receives absolutely nothing. I suggest to the minister that since his department has recognized the principle that the widow of a soldier with a disability of fifty per cent or more is entitled to pension, surely the same principle should be applied to all soldiers whether their disability is five, forty-five or sixty-five per cent. I sincerely hope the minister will give that suggestion very serious consideration and do something about it.
In conclusion, I wish to refer briefly to some of the remarks made this afternoon by the hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson) in dealing with the declaration made in this house by the present leader of the socialist party at the short session in December, 1939, when the hon. member for Rose town-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) placed on Hansard the policy of his party. While the member for York-Sunbury was speaking this afternoon he was interrupted by various members of the socialist party who stated that there were several statements on record showing that they had repudiated that stand. But let me point out that during last session, when bill No. 80 was introduced to amend the National Resources Mobilization Act, after a very long debate, when the vote was taken, every member of the socialistic party, for reasons known only to themselves, voted against that bill.

speechtext: It is just a matter of argument. I see no point of order in the contention of the hon. member for Weyburn.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I repeat that the socialistic party, in taking the stand which they did in the vote on bill No. 80, voted against the sending of men overseas to support the troops there. I have always contended that when this parliament decided to send an expeditionary force overseas there was an obligation not only on every member of this house but on every citizen of Canada that these boys must be supported with all necessary reinforcements, the finest implements of war, and everything else necessary, no matter what the cost might be.
I should also like to associate myself with the remarks made by the hon. member for York-Sunbury when he advocated a policy of private enterprise and personal initiative. It seems to me that only under such a policy is there any hope for our children or for the boys when they return from overseas. The men who serve in this war will have had enough of regulation and regimentation, and will be only too anxious to regulate their own affairs. It is quite true that the controls we have to-day are irritating, but they are absolutely nothing compared with the controls and regimentation to which we would be subject under a socialistic party. Freedom, absolute freedom, is one of the things for
which our boys are fighting to-day. We have in Germany an example of what happens in a socialistic state. There, instead of the state being subject to the will of the people, everyone was absolutely subject to regimentation and dictation by the state. I suggest that under the programme suggested by the socialistic party, whereby they would do away with private enterprise, there would be taken away from the youth of this country one of the biggest assets which youth has, namely, the ambition to succeed, to carve out a career for themselves, the right of each one to earn his own living under his own direction and to retain what he honestly earns and acquires, after the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) has taken his share. Take away this ambition to succeed and to carve out a career from the youth of this country, and you destroy one of the greatest assets youth has.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I hope that the hon. member for Hastings-Peterborough will not expect me to follow him in what seems to me was a rather distorted and inconsistent attitude in certain portions of his address. I desire at the outset to commend the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) for his great industry, loyalty, and devotion to duty. I intend to say very little about the budget, which is probably the greatest operation in the sphere of finance which Canada has ever known, but I am sure the people are grateful for having, in the person of the present minister, a man capable of doing the job. There is one matter in the budget to which I wish to refer, but the statements I intend to make are entirely upon my own responsibility. I refer to the allusions to the farmers and the income tax. The minister and his advisers have honestly, no doubt, attempted to meet the situation of the farmers, not realizing, I am sure, the position they hold in the national economy. The minister stated, as reported at page 849 of Hansard:
It will be difficult to put farmers on a pay-as-we-earn basis because it is so very hard for them to estimate their income in advance. We are proposing to give them as much latitude as possible by simply requiring them to pay two-thirds of their tax any time up to December 31 -on the basis of a rough guess or calculation- and the balance when they file their final return in March of the following year. Higher agricultural incomes have now brought many farmers into the taxable income ranges, and I am glad to know that the Department of National Revenue is making special efforts to assist the farmer in reckoning his income and calculating his tax.

The Budget-Mr. Ward

free. During the last election campaign I opposed conscription. I voiced my opposition throughout my constituency, and said I was doing so on my own responsibility. But had the Prime Minister and the government been in favour of conscription, I would still have been against it. Why? Not that I was against conscription as a principle; but I was irrevocably opposed to the conscription of flesh and blood while at the same time more material things were allowed to be given voluntarily, or when the people felt like doing so. We had an example during the last war, when a flock of millionaires were created out of war profits. I have been told that 138 millionaires were created during the last war, and in one or two of the post-war years. Whether that figure is correct, I cannot say; but we know that enormous profits were made.
We had that example, and the only one we had. Consequently I was opposed to conscription, until I knew something more about what was to be done by the government of Canada. I am now grateful to the government, particularly to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and the Minister of Finance, for the extent to which they have gone in conscripting wealth. Now that it has reached into the pockets of members of parliament; now that the income tax collector gets $800 or $900 from each of us, the argument is pretty well closed, so far as members are concerned.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: May I draw the hon. member's attention to the amendment moved at this session by the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation to the motion for an address in reply at this session, deploring the fact that the government has not conscripted wealth.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: "Where ignorance is bliss, 'tis folly to be wise."

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is true.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
If from eleven and a half million people the treasury can step up the revenue by nearly two billions of dollars in three years, then I think that is conscripting wealth with a vengeance. I cannot imagine any system of conscription my hon. friend would put into effect, involving the taking over of factories, farms, mines and all the rest, which wovdd leave behind it anything but chaos and liabilities, whereas the system we now have leaves behind it great assets.
I turn now to a statement made by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), as reported in the press on January 23. This is the report of a broadcast delivered at the time of the steel strike, at which time the hon.
member said that the arbitrary price and wage freezing policy adopted in this country decrees that men employed in that arduous and hazardous occupation should work for a wage that is demonstrably too low. I wonder if the hon. member has ever visited any of those steel mills. I have, on several occasions.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: And so has he.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I have been through several of .the larger Canadian steel mills, and so far as arduous labour is concerned-well, yesterday we were talking about cutting wood-a good wood chopper will cut about two cords of wood a day. A man who cuts and piles two cords of cordwood a day does at least four times as much work as any man I saw working in any steel mill I visited. There is no comparison. The work in a steel mill is not arduous; I saw nothing arduous about it. And the hon. member says it is hazardous. I was indeed struck by the perfect lighting of the buildings, and the almost perfect atmosphere of the place.
Then he went on to speak of the wages being low. What were the wages paid in those steel mills where the men were on strike? The payroll average-nothing to do with salaries to foremen or managers-was eighty-one cents an hour. I do not call that low pay. If I could have my wages frozen at eighty-one cents an hour for the rest of my life I should consider I was fairly lucky.
Then he went on to say that war planning and post-war policies were two parts of the same fight for victory, and that we are indeed building the post-war world now by the way in which we organize the war. I want the house to get this, because it shocked me. He said:
What can these men think of a war effort that does not hesitate to spend hundreds of millions of dollars to assist private industry?
He stops there. The hon. member knew just as well as I do that a meaner form of misrepresentation than that statement could not possibly have been made. Does he not know that war is expediency from the very battlefield where a general organizes his army to meet the enemy right back to the uttermost channel of our war effort? Truly the government are helping the industries. What for? To help our war effort. Helping them to build larger plants, to remodel their plants, to put in new machinery and tools and the myriad things that go to make up our war effort. Of course the government have helped, to the extent of hundreds of millions of dollars. But they have not given it to private industry, as the hon. member would have us believe.

The Budget-Mr. Ward
I should now like to come back to this table which I got from the bureau of statistics. One of the first things I did when I came here was to call up the bureau to get the average rate of pay in all the steel mills of Canada including the three where the men were then on strike. I obtained from the bureau the rate of wages paid in those three mills. I expected, of course, to find that the pay there was quite low. But that was not so; it was almost exactly on the level of the mill at Hamilton and the other mills throughout Canada. What is the fact? The average wage is $34.79 a week, or $1,809 a year, which is more than double what the average farmer in Canada receives, and this has been his best year. The shipyards of Canada are paying an average of $38.78 a week or $2,016 a year, which is about two and a half times the income of the average farmer. Aircraft factories are paying $35.50 a week, or $1,846 a year, which is again, more than double that earned by the average farmer.
I pause here to suggest to the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar and the hon. member for Weyburn that they go out and tell their farmer friends that they have been damning the government because they did not rush to the rescue of a group of striking men who were in receipt of an average of eighty-one cents an hour.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Will the hon. member permit a question? Has he also the average salary paid to the operators and owners?

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I will now come to the hon. member for York South. Speaking in the debate here a short time ago, the hon. member said:
There is a second feature of the government's fiscal policy with which we are in disagreement, namely, the level at which the government has found it necessary to freeze wages.
I simply repeat what I have already said; that if I could have my wages frozen at eighty-one cents an hour for the rest of my life I should consider myself secure for life. I think the men in the industrial organizations of Canada are the highest paid, except perhaps for the few in the United States, of any such employees in the world. It is time we recognized the fact that our industrial organizations are doing well by their employees.
I pause here to say that I noticed the other day where Mr. Mosher made a remark that soon the unions would have the employers of Canada under their heel. Well,
for years I talked about banks, mortgage companies, steel trusts and the like as being autocratic organizations that ruled the roost. But these people all had an investment in Canada; they had something to protect, something to guard.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Have not the
workers?

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Yes, they have their job to guard, but they do not guard it very well. I think we are just as safe under the heel of some of the steelmakers as we would be under the heel of an organized group of labourers who have no investment in the country. It seems to me we should be very cautious what we do in this regard. Labour unions are going much too far. I say to the government, that had I been the Minister of Labour or the Prime Minister when the steel strike took place, illegal as it was-there was really no difference between that strike and a great system of stealing; it was against the law of the land. The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) and, I suppose, the rest of his followers aided and abetted this illegal act on the part of these strikers. Had I been the government I would have given these men just twenty-four hours to be back on the job, and if they were not back I would have had a uniform there for every man the next morning. I would have said, You will either put on the uniform and go into the army at $1.50 a day the same as the other soldiers, or you will go back to work. There might have been a few heart failures, because men producing steel products, the all-important product in the winning of the war, going on strike in the middle of the war when they were getting eighty-one cents an hour, are too cowardly to fight, to go to war. Of course they are. There would have been a few heart failures and likely deaths. I think the Minister of Labour and the government showed wonderful patience and consideration for these men, and I hope there will be no more strikes during the period of this war.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: May I ask the hon. member a question? Did he offer a uniform to the manufacturers of this country in 1939 when they refused to manufacture war materials unless they got more than five per cent profit?

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I am not discussing that. I am not a manufacturer; I know nothing about the business, but I did have the privilege of discussing this whole question with a man who I think was perfectly honest. He is the manager of one of the largest concerns in Canada producing munitions of war. I said, "Why did you men refuse to accept war contracts on a
72537-87}
The Budget-Mr. Ward

five per cent basis?" He said, "We would all have been in the poor-house; we could not have lived." I asked why. He replied, "If you knew the government inspectors and the extent to which they reject material, you would understand that by the time they get through, our five per cent would be all gone. We are not making any money even at ten per cent." I am only repeating what this gentleman said; I am not arguing the point, because I do not think it is pertinent to the discussion at the moment. But I think those men who are getting the wages now being paid in the industries of Canada should at least remain on the job until the war is over.
I wras amazed the other day to hear the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar, the leader of the socialist group, repudiate the idea that he was a socialist or that he had any interest in collective ownership. I thought my hearing was fairly good, but after listening to the speeches that have been delivered by his followers I could hardly credit my ears. However, I thought I remembered a statement made by the hon. gentleman himself not long before which was rather incriminating. I looked it up, and here is what he had to say, as reported at page 1109 of Hansard:
However, the unfortunate factor is that in normal times the main stimulus to economic activity is not defence of the nation or the good of the community, but the making of profit.
We all know that he and his followers did not have a great deal of interest in the good of the community a few years ago, when we were struggling to lay the foundation for a war industry in this country. He continued:
To my mind that motive is wrong, but it is the motive which sets the wheels of industry in motion and keeps them running.
A little later he said:
The interest of the people is sacrificed in such times by non-government intervention-
Well Mr. Speaker that is the kind of government I want; I do not want the government to interfere with me. I want to carry on my farming enterprise according to my own good or bad judgment. He continued: -but that is the price we pay for free enterprise.
Well, Mr. Speaker, there are only two systems, not half a dozen. You must have either collective ownership, which is socialism, or private ownership. He continued:
We take the position that in any proper form of society human needs ought to come first and that the making of profit ought to be a purely secondary consideration. . . .
Let me go back to my own farm and my neighbour's farm. I shall be perfectly frank
and tell my hon. friends that I farm, first, to make a living for myself and my family, second, because I like farming, and, third, for profit, just as every other farmer farms for profit. I thought the late Hon. Norman Rogers put the whole case very well during the last session that brilliant gentleman was with us, when he said, "Yes, as a professor of economics I am socialistically inclined, but as I look around Canada and see the extent to which free enterprise has developed this country, and the progress it has made, I cannot believe that this country would become socialist-minded in less than two hundred years." I think he was about right. My hon. friend can put that in his pipe and smoke it. Let him go back home and think that over.
May I now come to the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis), and see what he thinks of collective ownership. As reported at page 164 of Hansard he said:
For the past two or three months these newspapers have consistently referred to the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation not as such but as the "socialist party." The socialist party is, of course, a left wing movement, and the Liberal party is a right wing movement, and therefore the Progressive Conservative party is going to get in the centre with a sound and sensible programme for the people of Canada.
He was worrying about that. A little later
on he said:
For at least twenty-five years I have had some knowledge of the different labour parties across Canada, from British Columbia to Nova Scotia.
I imagine he knows more about Ontario now, since I believe he spent most of last summer in this province. He continued-
I know that in 1932 they came to the realization that there was no solution for our problems in the provincial fields, and consequently men and women who were active over that period of time met in Calgary and examined the problem on a national basis and set up a national organization, because our problems are national and not provincial.
That was where the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation, a socialist party, was born. All through the speech there is this talk of socialism. He went on to say yes, that he was a socialist; he made no bones about it. That is the hon. member for Cape Breton South.
I come now to the hon. member for Wey-burn (Mr. Douglas), who said, as reported at page 510 of Hansard:
Therefore we believe that for anyone to talk, as the hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson) did yesterday about social security on
IMr. Ward.]

The Budget-Mr. Ward
the one hand and retaining free enterprise on the other is a contradiction in terms, because rugged individualism has never produced for our generation anything but ragged individuals on the one hand and people wallowing in wealth on the other.
I want to remind the hon. member that the farmers of his own province believe in rugged individualism, and if they are ragged it is because nature has been unkind or because they are unkind to themselves. Then he goes on, and his speech becomes even more interesting. He said:
It is time we realized that to talk glibly-
Imagine the hon. member for Weyburn blaming anyone for talking glibly!
-about "social insurance" and "social security" and the "Beveridge plan" as though these things could be superimposed upon an economic system that has produced poverty on the one hand and plenty on the other-
So that by implication the hon. member says we shall have to do away with private ownership and establish collective ownership before we can bring about these other things. In support of his arguments he quotes a Mr. Ryan of Washington., who in an article published in the United States said:
I do not believe that an economy dominated by the philosophy of "free enterprise" will be able to meet that demand.
Well, I do' not know what that means if it does not mean what it says.
I come now to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). I counted the number of times he used the expressions "common man" and "common people," and found that in one column he had used them ten times. The people to whom he refers, the farmers, the working men, the small merchants and so on, are not, to my mind, the common people. They are the aristocrats of our country, the people upon whom we must all depend, the people who do the work of the country. They are the real people, but he refers to them as the "common people." Perhaps on account of his profession he does not know who are the common people of this country.
To come back to the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation, the hon. member for Rose-town-Biggar said that if we progressed no more rapidly in the next twenty-three years than we have in the last twenty-three years, there will be little hope for the future of the social security plan. I wonder where he has been during the past twenty years? After all, social progress is not just social progress. Tremendous economic progress was made long before my hon. friends were heard of, even
before some of them were bom. As I say, great social progress has been made, and nearly all under Liberal governments.
Do we want to go back to where we were prior to the last war when there was no social legislation on any of the statute books of this country? I do not think hon. members are fair, either to themselves or to Canada, when they talk that way. I do not believe that New Zealand or Great Britain or any other country, Russia included, is any more sincere, any more capable mentally, or any more willing or desirous of making progress than is Canada. We do not have to go clear across the world to New Zealand to find a way of dealing with our social and economic problems. We shall deal with them here just as the people of Canada feel it is propitious to do so, as we feel we are able to do so and when we feel it is the proper time. If the great social security plan now before the committee reaches full fruition, I think Canada will be in a most enviable position as compared with that of most other countries.
It may be that our friends of the socialist group feel rather badly. They may think the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) has stolen their thunder. But that is not the case; he is just carrying out the programme which many of us have watched progressing for many years. I will confess something. I came into this house over twenty years ago as an opponent of the Prime Minister. I did not know him, and I came here with some preconceived notions of him. It was not because of anything that happened with anyone else; it was only because of what occurred between the Prime Minister and myself, but the fact is that the longer I have known him, the greater has my confidence in him and my respect for him become. Instead of maligning our own country and our own people and our own government, we would be doing more for ourselves, more for posterity if we got down on our knees and thanked God for having such a government as we have, a government with the understanding and the courage to do the things they are doing.
When the government embarked upon a price ceiling scheme they knew it would be unpopular. But they did it. They had the courage to do it. For whom were they doing it? It was done for the working people of Canada. They are the people who will profit and benefit by the continuity that will follow after the war, the stability we shall have then instead of the terrific distortions that followed the last war. I can remember in the third year of the last war when sugar sold in our town for $26 per 100 pounds. There was never
The Budget-Mr. Ward

any stoppage in the flow of raw sugar from the West Indies to Canada at that time. As there is to-day there were no sugar mills standing idle in those days, as there are at present but sugar went to $26 per 100 pounds. Why? Because of the mad inflation that occurred. But this government has kept the prices of sugar down to near what it was before the war.
What about clothing? During the last war I can remember paying $100 for a suit. I could not afford that, but I had to pay it. I needed a suit. There was no reason for such a price. As there was never a day when the fine soft wool from the south stopped coming to Canada. We had a smaller army to clothe, but the price of clothing went sky-high. Today one can go down to stores on Sparks street and buy a good suit of clothes for $35, the same price as he had to pay before the war. Why? Because we have a government that has had the courage to do the right thing -control prices.
I listened with interest the other day to the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Perley). I noticed that he was much more modest than usual, but he still got off the track two or three times. He criticized the government rather severely for not having done something about writing off soldier debts. He was a member of a party in power during five of the worst years agriculture has ever known in the history of Canada. There never was a time when the soldiers were more in need of their accounts being written off or written down, but very little was done during that period. He went on to tell us about his great interest in old age pensions. Old age pensions -were almost hoary headed when he came into this house. They have been in effect in this country since 1926, and I do not know why he should show an interest in something which was in effect for almost ten years before he became a member.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, since the beginning of this debate I have taken great interest in the speeches delivered by hon. members. Many of those speeches contained very good suggestions. Although I cannot agree with all that was said by my hon. friends, I have pleasure in mentioning especially the speeches of the leader of the Social Credit party (Mr. Black-more) and the leader of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation (Mr. Coldwell). Those two speeches contained many constructive suggestions, and I have no doubt that if the ministers would listen to some of the views expressed therein, it would assist
them in the performance of the difficult tasks they have to perform at the present time.
The remarks I intend to make on the budget and on the amendment will not be of the type used by masters of finance; they will be couched in the language of the man on the street. I must say that with a budget of $5,500,000,000 we are far from the moderate effort which was promised us by the leaders of the Liberal party during the 1940 election campaign. I cannot refrain from recalling this. Everybody knows that the government succeeded in obtaining the support of the province of Quebec because our people were told emphatically that, notwithstanding previous engagements, if the government had decided to participate in the war, it was very well understood that the participation would be a moderate one. We who opposed the Liberal party, tried to make the population understand that they were once more being duped, but the declarations of the leaders of the Liberal party were so emphatic that the people thought fit to give them their support. It was, I think, the first time in the history of mankind that a government decided to declare war against another country and at the same time maintained that they would make it just a smooth war. The people of Canada, remembering those engagements, and looking at the present budget, find that this smooth war has turned into a real war.
The second thing that comes to the mind of the man on the street is that this budget disregards too much the situation of the Canadian family. The exemptions provided for families with children are not adequate, especially when we take into consideration the obligations of those who have many children below the age of fourteen. I know that no one will be surprised to learn that in the province of Quebec, especially outside the cities, families of eight or nine children are numerous, and therefore it is in the province of Quebec that the burden will be heavier for the taxpayer. I have here an answer which was given to me in this house on the 15th instant regarding the 1941 census. It shows that families of five or more children, and especially those with seven or more, are found particularly in the province of Quebec. I shall give only a few figures to illustrate my point. They appear at page 1227 of Hansard of March 15 of this year. The table given there shows that there are in the dominion 98,500 families with five children. Of this number 34,340 families are in the province of Quebec. There are 63.240 families with six children, and of this number 25.760 are in the province of Quebec. Other figures show that there are 84,920 families with from seven to
[Mr. Ward.l

The Budget-Mr. Dorion
nine children each, and of this number 43,170 are in the province of Quebec. Then there are 20,890 families with ten or more children and of this number 13,220 are in the province of Quebec. I contend that if our objective is to do our utmost to win the war we must never forget that society in general for the safeguarding of which we are fighting is founded on the smaller society called the family, and if we have to protect the civil society we must of necessity bring our utmost protection to its essential element, namely, the family. I submit this point of view to the government. I believe that it will be necessary to review this part of the budget so as to give better protection to the heads of families. We should not take away from them the necessary means to provide for the raising of their children, and for this purpose they should enjoy a larger exemption from taxation.
The third point I raise is that it appears from the budget that the government does not take the money where it is, and here I cannot emphasize too much the statement of the leader of the Social Credit group when he said in this house, as reported at page 1091 of Hansard of March 9, 1943:
All the property of the people of Canada, particularly of the producers, is being mortgaged to a few Canadians. The bonds are gravitating into the hands of a very,- very few, as all the records tend to show.
Further on he said:
Those individuals are accumulating so many bonds that they will be able to live upon the interest of those bonds. . . . They will become a special class of gentlemen of privilege . . . they will control the laws of this country. They will control government policy. They will also control the banking policy of this country. Therefore, as I said a short time ago, from eighty to eighty-five per cent of all Canadians will become hewers of wood and drawers of water for the remaining fifteen per cent. They will be serfs.
The men who are now overseas . . . will come back here and become members of the serf class almost to a man.
I believe this statement is mostly true, and I do not hesitate to say that a system which brings about such a state of things is not sound.
But there is something more inconceivable. When it is a question of raising men for the war, we do not ask the soldiers, the sailors, and the airmen to lend their lives, at interest, to the country. We ask them to devote their youth and their energies, and even to give their lives to protect our country and our institutions. I cannot understand, and I know the people of this country cannot understand why, when it is a question of raising money, things should be altogether different. I cannot understand why we cannot ask those who
have the money, to give it for the protection of the country and for the safeguarding of their own capital. But instead we ask them to lend it, at interest. So that after the war those few people who already control finance will see their capital increased to a high degree. On the other hand, we shall see the soldiers come back home after having suffered, and many of them crippled, and we shall say to them: You have fought gallantly for your country, but now you will pay for the rest of your life the interest on the capital of those who lent their money to your country, and for the protection of which you have fought so hard.
I would also remind the government that I cannot accept the view of those who at the present time contend that if the government has found the way of raising money to produce so large a quantity of war materials, it will after the war easily find a way to provide the people of this country with the necessary means of living. I cannot accept this statement, and we must be very careful not to depend upon it, because I remember that twenty-five years ago we had a war which everybody remembers. The government at that time also succeeded in finding a way to provide our armies and our people with the necessities of life and the needs of war. Production was raised to a very high degree, and we believed then that the government had found a way to provide the people with the necessities of life after the war. This belief is substantiated by a statement which I find in the Sirois report, volume 1, at page 90, from which I quote:
The success with which the dominion government had organized a peaceful society for combat showed how governments could alter the conditions of economic and social life. If governments could organize so effectively for destruction, they should be able to organize the conditions of the good life for their citizens. Under the pressure of social inequalities which became more and more evident, this changing philosophy of the appropriate sphere of state activity led straight to extensive government intervention in economic life and to the provision and further extension of social services.
However, a few years after the war our country came through the gravest crisis we have ever known. Every one remembers the dark days of the period from 1930 to 1939. If after the last war the government of this country did not succeed in bringing to the people the necessary means of living decently, I cannot attach much importance to the declaration of those who to-day maintain that this war teaches us how to get wiser means of providing for the people in the future the necessary' means of life.
The Budget-Mr. Dorion

I believe the burdens of the war would be and; should be lessened, by preventing gifts or loans to countries much more wealthy than we are. I do not hesitate to declare that I cannot understand how the people of Canada, bearing on their shoulders a heavier burden than any other allied country, can, be called upon to help another country which is doing things like those that have been disclosed not long ago. We find, in the Magazine Digest of February, 1943, at page one, an article condensed from the Banker, of London. This article is entitled "A bank whose money we can do without." It is written by Mr. Paul Einzig, who is at the present time foreign editor of the Financial News and the Banker, in London. It deals with a bank called the Bank of International Settlements. I quote:
From the very first day of the war, private citizens and firms in Britain were ordered to sever all connections with those neutral firms which had been put on the black list because they were controlled by enemy interests. Failure to comply is severely punished. But the Bank of England seems to be an exception. Certain of its directors are allowed, even in 1942, to remain on the board of a bank the share capital of which is held by axis-controlled interests to the extent of seventy-two per cent.
And further on:
It is almost impossible to say whether any axis assets in this country, in the United States of America or in Latin America have escaped being frozen because they were camouflaged as Bank of International Settlements assets. . . .
Further, if we look at the composition of the board, we find that out of sixteen directors, only two are British and two neutral, while the remaining twelve are nationals of axis or axis-controlled countries.
This question was raised in the British House of Commons on October 13, 1942. In commenting on the debate, the article states:
The very situation, with whose description Sir Kingsley Wood sought to make the flesh of M.P.'s creep on October 13: would then arise.
If, as he emphatically claimed, the withdrawal of British directors from the B J.S. would result in substantial advantages for the axis and grave disadvantages for the allies, why doesn't Germany bring about that situation by exercising the powers conferred by the axis control over the majority of voting rights at the shareholders' meeting and on the board of directors?
Instead, the Germans even continue paying interest on their debt to the B.I.S. after having defaulted on so many other financial obligations. Why? Because it obviously suits them to tolerate the neutrality of the B.I.S. and to secure the continued British participation in it, even at the cost of sacrifices.
And the last part I quote is this:
Since Germany is in a position to assume full control but prefers to tolerate British participation and "neutral" control, it would obviously be to her disadvantage, and therefore to the advantage of the united nations, if that
country took the initiative in terminating its relations with the Bank of International Settlements.
The man on the street, the man who works hard to help the war effort of his country, cannot understand such a state of affairs; and I believe the government should give some explanation before asking us to give our money or lend it to a country in which some people are doing business with the enemy. I be- . lieve also that the government does not pay enough attention to the actual needs of our country, and- that it should not withhold expenditures necessary to provide the country with the ordinary means of communication.
Speaking for the constituency which I have the honour to represent, I take it as a duty to advise the government that there are on the north coast of the St. Lawrence many small harbours which will not be utilized any longer if the government does not provide them with the necessary repairs to the wharves or does not undertake the necessary dredging.
I receive every week news from different parts of my constituency, advising me to that effect; and if our fishermen cannot be provided with suitable harbours they will not be able to perform their usual tasks and the country as a whole might be deprived of the results of the work they used to do.
I wish also to draw the attention of the government to the question of transport to and from these new vast industrial areas of Chicoutimi and lake St. John where lately a dam was built at the cost of 865,000,000.
At the present time there is only one railroad linking these industrial areas with the rest of the country. Since it is an old railroad it happens very often that the carrying of war materials is delayed on account of a broken rail or some other defects. The passenger trains have been reduced to three a week although, according to the last census, the population of this area is about 20,000 more than it was a few years ago.
There would be one way to correct this situation, and I think the government should listen very carefully to the following suggestion. It would be the building of a railroad between Murray Bay and Chicoutimi, a distance of about sixty-six miles. This would complete a belt-line from Quebec to Chicoutimi. I know this question has already been studied, and that around 1917 there was a survey showing the possibility of this project, which if it were realized would be of a great help to the war effort of this country in establishing much better means of com-, munication between the war plants of lake St. John district and the rest of the country.

The Budget-Mr. Donion
It would also be of great advantage after the war for the development of this part of the country; and as I said in my speech on the address in reply to the speech from the throne, the government should pay special attention to these works that will be as useful in peace time as they are in war time.
I must add that it would also be fair for the province of Quebec to have this railroad added to those we already have, because, according to the statistics, we find that the province of Quebec is the one in which the proportion of railroads is less than in any other province according to the area and the population.
Therefore I urge the government to consider this project, and I am convinced that they will easily come to the conclusion that it constitutes one of the good suggestions that could be made at the present time.
(Translation) Mr. Speaker, I have tried to state as briefly as possible what the man in the street thinks of the budget now before us.
I must add that even in many industrial and business circles there is a feeling of justified uneasiness about the size of this budget. Thus, the bi-monthly bulletin issued by La Banque Canadienne Nationale, for January and February, 1943, contains the following comments:
An increase in the production of armaments is being contemplated again this year. But labour and raw materials now available in this country are so reduced that any such increase in that field will entail a further lessening of activity in numerous establishments catering to the needs of the civilian population and even in certain basic industries.
And further on:
Despite what has been achieved since the outbreak of war, food production is still inadequate in this country which is called upon to supply various foodstuffs to the armies and the civilian population of Great Britain and other united nations. That is why there is such an insistent demand for more consignments of our meats, eggs, dairy products and various other commodities. Now, Canadian farms, which military service and employment in war industries have deprived of about 250,000 farmers and farm workers since the beginning of 1940, are to-day facing a labour shortage the seriousness of which it would be dangerous to overlook. The restrictions imposed on farm implement factories whose production this year must not exceed 24 per cent of the 1940 figure, will add to the difficulties of the situation.
It is consequently imperative that some way be found of ensuring an adequate production of foodstuffs, since the latter are the most essential war munitions.
It is admitted even by those financial interests that we are now facing a situation which is becoming more and more alarming and it may be wondered what will happen if the war is to last many years longer and whether we shall always succeed in devising ways and means of meeting both our war requirements and the needs of our civilian population.
I wish to take this opportunity to express the feelings of all right-minded Canadians who witness to-day with deep concern the social disruption brought about by the employment of women in industrial plants.
It is not difficult to see that we are now preparing a generation that will suffer untold harm from the fact that women have been so ill-advisedly called upon to assume a share of the hard and tiring work performed in the shops. I do not hesitate to say that no medical specialist can possibly deny that working in a shop, night and day, among noisy machines, cannot but upset the nervous system of a woman and make her an easy prey for every kind of disease, especially tuberculosis.
Archbishops and bishops gave warning throughout the land. Medical societies echoed their uneasiness and all who would see a decent social and economic life maintained in our country are deeply worried by the part which women are taking in industrial activities.
This question is so important that the government should have a serious inquiry undertaken by competent men and themselves take such remedial steps as are necessary to correct the present system.
I feel in duty bound to quote briefly from an article by the Rev. Father Alexandre Dugre, S.J., presenting the best and most substantial argument on the subject:
Following their conscience rather than their interest doctors have denounced the terrible epidemic. I have treated healthy girls, says one, with a build as tall and strong as a man's, who were absolutely ruined after a year and a half, a record. They lived in an oppressive atmosphere and surrounded by a pandemonium of noise. Nervous overstimulation caused stomach and heart disorders.
And further on:
Soldiers will die or return, but women in the army or munitions plants will not quite die and yet they will never recover. They will never be the same. Something within shall have snapped. Woman intended to be a temple must never become a shop.
Still further on I find this:
When directors of the selective service and leaders in this country themselves proclaim that "the housekeeper, a front line trooper on the

The Budget-Mr. Dorion

home front, carries on essential war work" (Mr. Goulet); that "disorganization of the home for the benefit of industry, far from helping the war effort, hampers it, delays it, and endangers our future" (Mrs. Eaton); that "women in the home no less than those in the shop make a direct contribution toward the preservation of that civilization which our enemies would destroy" (Mr. King),-they are right. We ask that action be in keeping with such splendid statements and that our readers cooperate by remaining at home, rendering the really great service which is expected from civilized women.
And finally:
In this war where we count so little, we put up with inconveniences, rationing and sacrifices. We supply the money, we give our sons, our blood. But wre shall not sacrifice our women: it would mean setting ourselves back twenty centuries. That Hitler may be broken, some better means must be found than breaking up our homes by adding to the long roll of martyrs in the shops.
I cannot believe that the government shall not heed the almost desperate appeals coming from our doctors and economists and I trust a thorough study of this question will be undertaken immediately.
There is another matter which I would like to mention. This budget before us is the most formidable assault ever launched upon provincial autonomy.
There will come another opportunity for me to discuss this matter fully, but I wonder if we are not witnessing the application of the projects contained in the Sirois report which, as everyone knows, was rejected at the time of the interprovincial conference which was called to consider it.
Mr. Speaker, before closing my remarks I wish to say that I cannot support the amende ment moved by the leader of the Social Credit group. In fact, while I am in agreement with most of the suggestions contained in this amendment, I do not think it would be proper for the government to control private business factories, farms, and other means of production. If some distinction had been made with regard to these so-called means of production, I might have agreed that the government could control some of them; but they would have to be distinctly described.
I cannot agree either to paragraph (e) of the amendment. I will admit that rationing is necessary, but I contend that it should be more adequately put into force throughout the dominion. If, instead of the words "aggressive and consistent", the word "adequate" had been used, I would have been ready to support it.
I believe, however, the subamendment moved by the leader of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation reflects the general sentiment of the population of this country, and therefore I am pleased to say that I do not hesitate to support it.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, rising for the first time, and perhaps for the last time while you are in the Chair, may I at the outset offer to you, sir, my hearty and warm congratulations upon the high office you have attained.
Rising to- say a few words regarding the budget so ably presented on the second day of this month, and in the fourth year of the war, I consider it my duty and honour to say I am of opinion we have one of the best and ablest ministers of finance we have ever had. Particularly, sir, do I wish to pay that tribute to our minister on behalf of many groups of people in my constituency, labour organizations and the like, who were so desirous of having a pay-as-you-go income tax plan put into effect. This has been done, and we are all very well pleased.
However, there is one thing I want him to do-and this is all I am going to say about it -namely, to fix up the old age pension and to do it quickly.
I need not remind you, sir, because you have been here many years longer than I have, and I have heard it said many times in this chamber, that the west has asked time and time again for more factories, more industrial plants. I mention it now for this reason, that a committee has recently been set up here to study the problems of rehabilitation and reconstruction. Judging from the personnel of that committee, we shall have a progressive and worthwhile report on the industrial needs and opportunities of western Canada which will be well studied by that committee. I would refer to the Defence Industries Limited plant near Transcona which is in my own riding; I do not want to see this plant closed down or salvaged immediately after the war.
