The same can be said of many plants all through western Canada. I hope at least to have a chance to obtain for the constituency which I represent some plants for western Canada. In my opinion it would be a shame and a disgrace to see that fine plant, in which two or three thousand men are employed, shut down and those men thrown out of work at the end of the war. I wish to pay tribute to those men for the fine work they are doing in this war effort, because we must remember that they were taken from the villages, the municipalities and the country; that many of them never saw the inside of a plant before,
[Mr. Dorion.)

The Budget-Mr. Turner
and that they are doing a splendid job, and it is my pleasure to pay them this little tribute to-night. When the war is over, these men will have had these years of extra experience and be fully prepared and equipped to carry on in similar capacities after the war. Therefore I urge with all the strength I have that that part of western Canada be kept in mind by the committee and the government. We should like to see that plant turned into a synthetic rubber plant or a plant for the manufacture of synthetic gasoline or plastic products, but certainly not destroyed and all those men turned loose to find other jobs.
I hope this government will not allow any immigration into this country after the war until at least all our returned men are taken care of; they should have first call and preferred jobs.
There is something not quite right in regard to our western industrial set-up when one considers even casually the immense possibilities for industry in the prairie provinces. Consider it only from the point of view of natural resources; look at what we have to offer industries: coal, timber, oil, the natural gas of Alberta in untold quantities, thousands of units of unharnessed electrical power, minerals of all kinds, and in my own constituency that new chromium deposit now in the experimental stage. It is well advanced; I believe 200 tons have been shipped. If this proves successful, I understand this will be the biggest development in recent years in Manitoba. These are only a few of the many things we have to offer. We have two of the best equipped and managed railways in the world to take care of the needs of industry. Behind all that we have great agricultural production in all its branches, capable of supplying a population five or ten times, possibly fifteen times what we have now, with the finest food this world can produce. There is only one answer, more and more factories because, if you get the factories, you get the population.
Speaking in this house on January 29 of last year about conditions on the farms as I saw them in my own constituency, I said, as reported at page 148 of Hansard:
During the harvest period last fall I took a trip through part of my riding, and on one farm I saw a poor old lady, sixty-five years of age, on top of a grain stack, working away there when she should have been at home listening to the radio or at least doing some easier job. On another farm, on the next section, I saw a little girl twelve years of age driving the tractor, while her father operated the power binder behind. He told me that he had tried his best to get help, offering $4 a day. but had not been able to secure it. That little girl should have been out playing. I am sure she must have been tired at night.
7253?- 88}
That problem is now more acute than ever, as a result' of the military call-up policy. There is hardly a day that I do not receive some complaints, particularly from the Tyndall and Melrose sections. I should like to read them to the house but I know the government must, by now, be aware of the situation. Let me, however, put this question to the government: Could you expect a young man who is the only boy at home, with three sisters, his father far from well-he has a doctor's certificate-to have in his mind a good, honest, clean thought about our war effort when he is taken into the army, leaving his sisters at home to look after thirty or forty head of stock when it is forty below zero, when he has been doing nothing but that job ever since he was old enough to drive a team of horses?
The principle that in this war agriculture is considered a major industry, along with munitions plants and the like, has, I think, been admitted on all sides of the house. Then why should not the solution of this farm labour problem be tackled along the same lines as [DOT] in the case of any other war industry? Having said that, I would impress upon the government with all the strength and ability I have the need to remedy this serious situation, and the sooner the better.
In the extract which I have just quoted from my speech of January 29, I referred to the long hours which both young and old and even partly invalided people have to put in and the hardships which they have to suffer on the farms ini Canada in order to keep up our war effort. They will continue to do so until the victorious end; we can depend on that. Therefore I make a suggestion to the government, and it is only a suggestion. It is this, that a part or all of the government's share of the excess profits tax taken since it was first started, on such companies only as use in their manufacture the basic products of the farm, for instance, malting companies, brewers, distillers, milling companies, bread companies, packers, elevator companies, should be held in trust by the government until the war is over and given back to the farmers of Canada, from whose hard toil it originated. This should be done because I believe the farmer is the one and only man who is coming out of this war on the wrong side of the whole show. This money would come at a time when he could use it for replacements, and the payment of debts incurred during the period of the war. It might be regarded as some kind of compensation plan to help these farm people for the long hours put in in all kinds of weather, who shifted from' one line of production to another as requested by the government. It would help the farmer to get
The Budget-Mr. Turner

back to his proper position. It appears to me from a labour point of view that somewhere in that excess profits tax must be found some relief for the farmer. He should have the first call on some of that money after the war.
May I now be permitted to proceed to another subject, a subject I had hoped I would never have to speak on while a member of this house, namely, the restrictions on beer, particularly during a war session when there are so many matters of real importance to discuss. I always understood that this matter had been definitely settled years ago as far as any action by the federal government was necessary. But it seems that "to beer or not to beer" is now the question. I assure you, sir, that whatever I may say on the matter is said for no other reason than that I deem it my public duty as a member of this house, and as a result of the many protests I have received from farmers, industrial workers, business and professional men, municipal officials, and from my own study and observations. This matter is becoming more serious every day and, if allowed to continue much longer, will do great harm to our people.
In the first place, let me say that beer rationing is nothing new here in Canada. It has been in effect for many years, since just after the last war, under provincial government control, by means of the permit system. Years ago, and even to-day, your liquor permit was tonsidered to be your ration book. The people of Canada want to know why beer should be further rationed. Who asked for it? Was it any of the members of the three armed services? I should not expect so. Was it anybody from the war veterans' associations or clubs? I have never heard that. Was it any labour group or any organization affiliated with labour? Not to my knowledge. Was it the Canadian federation of agriculture, or anyone else connected with agriculture? I have never been told that. I am sure it was not any of the provincial governments, because that is their main source of revenue. They might have agreed to it later, but they did not ask for it. It was not asked for by any authoritative body. The truth of the whole matter is that some group of prohibitionists and clergymen, mainly from Ontario, were the instigators of the whole thing. This group was headed by some representatives of the Ontario temperance federation, and they managed to exert enough pressure on our government to bring about this action. As a result, we have the present chaotic condition in the beer business.
Let me take one thing at a time, and let me ask what I think is a fair question. Did that body of men wrho came here to ask the government to take this step tell the government that they would take full responsibility for the result of any action taken along this line? I venture to say they did not. I imagine they were like the handle on the pot; yes, we shall be there, but we shall not be in it. Such prohibitionists are men with one-track minds, and if you examine them very closely you will find that this track is not of standard gauge, but is the old, obsolete narrow gauge. Democracy is slipping a little in this country when a minority group, who have failed in their chosen mission of convincing the multitude by means of religious education, can by government action impose their will upon the majority.
You will notice, Mr. Speaker, that I have used the word "labour" frequently. I have done so because beer is known the world over as the working man's drink, as the poor man's beverage, and in many instances his only form of relaxation. I can speak with some authority on that point. For almost ten years I was a hotel keeper in the industrial section of Winnipeg, right down near the Canadian Pacific tracks. Many of the men who are now working in plants engaged solely in war work told me many times that they had never attended a show or watched a baseball game in their lives, and never would; that their only pleasure and relaxation, the only thing they got out of life, was sitting down in the beer parlour with a few of their friends, drinking a glass of beer, talking politics and condemning the government. This country is at war, and conditions are not normal. They will not be normal for some time, but these prohibitionists have no regard for that. They always were and always will be opportunists who will attack when the time suits them, regardless of the outcome; and truer words were never spoken. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) addressed the nation over the radio on December 16 last in connection with this question of temperance and the war effort. I have a copy of that address in my hand, and nowhere did the Prime Minister tell us who demanded that beer should be rationed. Perhaps he thought we should know. That is why thousands of our people were stunned by the action taken by the government. Naturally they are asking many questions, because they believe this is only a short cut to what happened during the last war, namely, total prohibition. The members of this house and the people of this country know very well what happened as a result of that action.

The Budget-Mr. Turner
Therefore is it any wonder that the advertisement which I hold in my hand was published in all the newspapers in Canada? I will read it into Hansard in order to correct the false propaganda that has been circulated by temperance people:
Some plain talking about the beer shortage
Q. What is the extent of the shortage?
A. The available supply of beer under the new regulation is less than seventy per cent of to-day's demand with the expectation that the demand will become greater as time goes on.
Q. What has caused the shortage?
A. The dominion cabinet by order in council has restricted the quantity of beer which may be sold between November 1, 1942, and October 1, 1943.
Q. Why did the cabinet do it?
A. It is believed that the cabinet did it without careful study and principally to placate the prohibitionists who, by means of a powerful lobby, misrepresented conditions to the Prime Minister.
I agree with that.
In placating that element of society the government was placating the same class of people who years ago did everything they could to prevent Sunday street cars, who more recently have denounced the sending of beer to the very soldiers who, in the blistering heat of North African deserts, were fighting to preserve the liberties of the people back home; and who in their narrow-mindedness have effectively blocked proposals to have our picture theatres opened on Sundays for the benefit of enlisted men on weekend leave, who also even spread the false story-
I will come to this a little later; it is really good.
-that sugar is used in the brewing of beer in Canada.
Q. Was it necessary?
A. Beer has long been regarded the people's drink in the free democratic countries of the world. Canadian consumption has been low in relation to consumption in Great Britain and the United States. In 1942 Canada consumed 100,000,000 imperial gallons, equivalent to 1-3 pints per capita per week. The United States consumed 1,750,000,000 imperial gallons-
They can. really drink it over there.
-equivalent to 2-0 pints per capita per week. Great Britain consumed 700,000,000 imperial gallons, equivalent to 2-3 pints per capita per week. Beer is brewed from Canadian ingredients which are in plentiful supply and not required for the war effort. Canadian beer contains no sugar. Tea, coffee and sugar are transported to Canada by sea and their curtailment has been made necessary only by a shortage of ocean shipping.
Q. What will be the consequences?
A. Many of the evils of the prohibition era will return. Many of our soldiers, sailors, airmen and war workers are already being deprived of the nourishment and relaxation provided by a glass of beer.
Q. What is the remedy?
A. In a democracy a government is the servant of its people. Governments are not infallible and from time to time, acting on
bad advice, make mistakes. Whereas they should be quick to correct such mistakes, experience has shown that they are slow to do so unless the force of overwhelming public opinion makes itself known. The remedy in this case, therefore, is in the hands of the people of Canada, who believe in tolerance and moderation, to take every opportunity to publicly and privately express themselves against the government's too drastic restriction of the sale of beer. Otherwise a fanatical minority will be able to continue to impose its wishes upon the tolerant majority. In the last war (1914-18) the British government cut the production of beer but the indignation of the munition workers was so great that it had to be restored in order to maintain production.
Q. Have we published this advertisement because we face the loss of profits?
A. Emphatically no. This company's profits are not at stake because we are even now heavily into the 100 per cent excess profits tax category and any additional volume would only further wear out our plant without any compensation to our shareholders. We are making the fact known because we sincerely believe that the present shortage of beer is unnecessary and is not in the interests of true temperance, the maintenance of morale, and war production.
Canadian Breweries Limited.
In all fairness to the Prime Minister I must admit that one reason he gave for the cut was the labour problem, absenteeism and that sort of thing. Then it was said that an eight-hour day was sufficient for the sale of beer. That step already had been taken in my own province by the liquor control commission, with the full cooperation of the brewers and the hotel keepers. They voluntarily reduced the hours of sale from thirteen to eight; but the chaotic condition in which we find ourselves to-day did not result from the reduction in the hours of sale. It was brought about by the action of the government here in Ottawa. The hotel keepers are unable to get sufficient beer to enable them to keep open for eight hours, and now we have a new national anthem: "To beer or not to beer." The city hotels in particular are trying to operate on a "hit or miss-now you see it; now you don't" schedule because they have not sufficient beer on hand for the eight hours, and some days they do not have any at all. I am quite aware that it will be argued that the cut i3 thirty per cent now in order to get down to a ten per cent cut later on. But by that time the regular flow of business will have been diverted elsewhere. In many instances it has already gone elsewhere, and1 I am informed that this city is no exception.
This does not solve the problem in any way because to-day there is an increasing demand for beer. Can you imagine, sir, the condition we would find ourselves in if we followed the same course with respect to gas rationing? I think that is a good illustration. Can you imagine the chaos there would be if you
The Budget-Mr. Turner

called for gas at three o'clock in the afternoon and were told there was not any? I know the gas stations close at seven o'clock in the evening, but by that time everyone has been able to get the gas he needs. That is only one side of the story.
Here is another side. Look at what is happening to the ordinary citizen of this country who wants beer at home. In Ontario you used to be able to get a permit for twenty-five cents, but no more. It now costs you 82. I do not blame the government if it is in need of revenue; that is bad enough. In Quebec they now charge a non-resident fifty cents, and stamp his registration card on the back. But that is not all. In Alberta I am informed they intend to mark the conviction on the back of a man's national registration card if he is convicted of trying to obtain more than one permit. It is quite conceivable to expect in the very near future that we shall be required to have our photographs and finger-prints taken. Is this the kind of justice for which we are fighting? I do not think that sort of thing belongs with democratic ideas.
Is it any wonder that liquor stores are being robbed and doors and windows smashed, as reported occurred recently in Lethbridge? The remedy is simple. If a labour problem exists that makes it necessary to cut down, for heaven's sake make it eight or nine hours a day, but make sure that the public will be served during those hours. There should be sufficient beer on hand to serve everyone and not have us running around like a bunch of scared jack rabbits from one beer parlour to another. I am sure that if this reasonable request had been made of the provincial governments concerned in the first place, a favourable reply would have been received the next morning.
We are engaged in a world war where there is to be no saw-off to keep steady and cool at all times; we. must keep our feet firmly on the ground. We must expect that our nervous strain and high tension will continue and sometimes be near the cracking point. It will be tougher this year than ever before if I understand the Prime Minister correctly. Therefore, is it not only right, fair and reasonable that the government, as well as all public-minded bodies and groups, should do as little as they possibly can to disturb, interfere, or irritate in any way the day-to-day life of the ordinary common people, who, after all, are the ones who really drink and enjoy their glasses of beer. I think that is a sound statement to make.

The United States are making a magnificent war effort, and there has been no drastic cut in beer there. They drink more per capita than we do. That country remembers only too well the era of gangsters, racketeers and kidnapping through which they passed. Canada was not exempt from the same troubles. Let me state at once that I believe it is partly due to that disastrous period through which this country also passed that we find in this country, where there is an abundance of food, where there is everything to make it the best and healthiest place in the world to live, that in order to get 1,000 men for the services we must call up approximately 2,000 men. I can understand that condition existing when for years thousands of our people were unable to get a clean, wholesome glass of beer, properly served, on account of the actions of a similar group or their forefathers. They were forced to drink vanilla extracts, moon, uppercut, redeye and paint remover. I am surprised that the percentage of rejections is not even greater.
A new industry was then born in Canada. It still continues and probably will continue forever, and from it this government gets no revenue. One cannot forget that terrible episode which happened during the Christmas holiday season in Winnipeg when some fifty or more persons were taken at one time to the general hospital, two or more persons died and the rest just pulled through suffering from the effects of having taken canned heat. These people just pulled through, and we all still remember the stink of Hoffman drops all over the country. These things should be remembered.
My suggestion to the government at this stage is to stay on the beam and leave good enough alone. They should not interfere with the beer business, the working man's drink. Beer is the only alcoholic drink sold on draft for ten cents in Canada, and it can therefore be correctly labelled the working man's drink. The art of brewing is over six thousand years old, and there has never yet been found a substitute for beer. Let us then stop trying, until at least the war is won and victory has been secured.
This government has been criticized and bombed day and night from all altitudes as a result- of the numerous controls it has imposed upon the people. Why should it take on something which was not asked for or which is not necessary? It has been condemned for passing too many orders in council. Here is one, No. 11374, which it should suspend or cancel immediately in so far as it affects

The Budget-Mr. Turner
beer, the working man's drink. You can always trust the working man with his beer. There is no shortage of grain or other materials used in the manufacture of beer, because, after all, it is about ninety per cent water.
Contrary to the belief held by some in Canada, I think it can be argued successfully that there has been no great increase in the per capita consumption of beer. The plain fact is that there are more people drinking beer in Canada than ever before. I believe that is a good sign. If people must drink, it is much better for them to drink beer. In this connection I should like to read an extract from an article written by a doctor of this province, a superintendent of a large institution. It was handed to me just a little while ago, and it reads:
I don't think the government is doing a very good thing by restricting beer so much. The people, especially the working people are resenting it. They will stand for almost any restriction cheerfully if it is necessary but they have the idea in this case that the restriction was put on just because the government allowed itself to be stampeded by a few prohibitionists. There is certainly no shortage of grain in the country and the hard liquor distilleries can look after the alcohol. Strikes me as being one of the best times to really convert this country from hard liquor to beer. I suppose it is true that consumption has gone up in the last few years, but then again many poor devils are able to buy beer now that never were before, and incidentally able to buy bonds and stamps in quantities that they couldn't have touched three years ago.
_ It has been stated by the same group as part of their false propaganda that there is no food value in beer. I have here a letter which was written to the Free Press by Mr. Kensington Downes, a former member of the legislative assembly of Manitoba, and which I think will answer that once and for all. I shall not read it all, but I wish to read the last paragraph, in which Mr. Downes was answering an argument put forth by Doctor Cooper. This paragraph reads:
If, in the opinion of Dr. Cooper, beer is harmful, how does he account for the following? Plight Officer C. P. L. Streatfeld, Squadron Leader A. K. Passmore and Pilot Officer S. G. Turney, of the R.A.F. voyaged from Java to Australia in a twenty-eight foot lifeboat. They and nine companions subsisted for forty-four days on 960 cans of beer (pints) which they found in the lifeboat. They had neither a morsel of food nor a drop of water, yet they are alive and well.
The same outfit to which I have referred has condemned the sale of beer because the oreweries use large quantities of sugar. The fact is that no sugar is used in the manufacture of either beer or ale. Should I remind the government to beware of false witnesses? Perhaps these people are trying to catch a spot on the Fibber McGee programme. I have yet to see a sack of sugar in a brewery. However, I am not surprised at that outfit making that statement because in my opinion they could not tell a bottle of beer from the Empire State building.
How many times has it been said on the floor of this house that our army is the finest and the best equipped in the world? I join with others in that tribute. It has also been stated time and again by members on all sides of the house and by the Prime Minister himself, and with just pride, that our industrial production on all fronts, agriculture, implements of war, shipbuilding and so forth is greater now than at any previous time in our nation's history. How then can it be intelligently argued that beer restrictions were imposed on account of delays, absenteeism, and so forth? The very opposite is true. Under present conditions the worker has almost to take a day off in order to get a glass of beer. The case of the prohibitionists collapses completely in the face of the statement that I have just made.
The magnificent tributes that I have just mentioned as being paid to our armed forees were paid in the first place to our soldiers, sailors and airmen, but also to labour on the railways, for example, to the men who at forty degrees below zero make the railways safe for us to get here; to the skilled workers in the munitions plants; to the farmers and the fishermen; and to all those engaged in working in the mines and forests of our country. These people constitute the very backbone of Canada, and that they have done a magnificent job is admitted by all, including our own Prime Minister and Mr. Winston Churchill. They are by far the largest consumers of beer in Canada. Therefore, why should beer be rationed to them under pressure from a certain group of prohibitionists whose only contribution to the winning of this war, as far as I can judge, is in trying to stir up "internal combustion" in this country?
I have just mentioned that great leader, Mr. Churchill. It reminds me of the remark he made to General Montgomery when he met him in North Africa. He asked General Montgomery how he felt and the general replied, "One hundred per cent fit," and went on to say that he neither drank nor smoked. Churchill replied that he both drank and smoked and felt two hundred per cent fit. I also recall a statement of a man in whom my hon. friend the member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) will be very much interested because he became a famous judge I am told.
The Budget-Mr. Turner

This man said, "Before I have my ale I see things as they are, but after I have my ale I see things as they should be." I see my good friend the hon. member for Weyburn (Mr. Douglas) smiling. I have known him for a number of years.
May I digress at this point to pay a supertribute to the officers and all those who assisted them on the war loan committee, and certainly to every person in Manitoba for their combined efforts in sending that province over the top first in the last victory loan drive.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, to keep the record straight and up to date as far as Manitoba is concerned regarding beer rationing, let me say now that in that province we have had four local option contests since the war began, and in all four contests the people voted wet by a majority of two to one. Surely that does not look very much as if they wanted any restrictions on beer there.
At this point may I pay a tribute to the hotel keepers of my province and the trade generally, who through maintaining a high standard of public service were in part responsible for that good majority in those four local option contests.
Why should we in Manitoba be penalized by some false propaganda prohibitionists when the people themselves there have voted as I have already indicated and shown plainly what they want. We rebel and protest against this, and Ottawa will soon know it because Winnipeg has been circulated with cards to be signed and sent here, and this is only the beginning.
Why did not these prohibitionists whose grief, if they had any, was supposed to originate around the Jarvis street section of Toronto, use their own forces in calling for a local option vote or for any number of them, thereby localizing the problem if there was any? But they had different ideas. They wanted to head out for total prohibition with its multiple troubles. They wanted to go for the jack-pot. They wanted to establish total prohibition while the war was on and press the government to use the War Measures Act, and they intended to do it by any kind of sales talk, false or otherwise. In any event they won the first round and the government did pull the main switch, so that to-day we find all Canada, including my own good province of Manitoba, sent hurtling down the hill toward total prohibition where she lay twenty-five years ago and from which she has never recovered fully; her wounds are not yet fully healed. That is the story as I see it.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, having some knowledge of the situation to-day, may I ask the
government before it is too late, and with all the sincerity and strength that I possess, to immediately rescind or cancel order in council No. 11374 in so far as it affects beer, in order to offset the present move toward total prohibition which, in the light of past experience, would not only undermine governments, both provincial and federal, but certainly destroy the morale of our citizens of all classes, who possibly never before in their life broke the law of the land but will certainly rebel against restrictions of this kind, which are not necessary and may unfortunately cause them to become law breakers.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member (Mr. Turner) who has just taken his seat has just made probably the best delivery he has ever made in this house, but he rather disproved his case since he did it all on water.
Returning to the budget-from the ridiculous to the sublime-one's first impression on looking at the 1943 budget is that it proposes no great changes in our approach to financing Canada in a time of stress. The rates of taxation on incomes, individual and corporation, the excess profit tax and the sales tax remain practically the same. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) has adopted some principles of what is known as the Ruml plan, the pay-as-you-earn policy, and as a result those individuals who are paying taxes will find that their tax payments will be increased this year probably fifty per cent over what they paid last year. That is a disturbing consideration, but it is one of the consequences of the partial adoption of the Ruml plan. The minister outlined many of its advantages, but I would point out that there are also a great many disadvantages. In the first place the tax is based on an income which is unknown. Experience has shown that the income of a nation can vary considerably over a twelvemonth period. An accurate estimate of the nation's income is impossible. Second, there are certain classes of income which cannot be taxed at the source. Payments on unregistered bonds and1 certificates, certain collections and note payments, cannot be closely watched unless revenue officers are to be in every office. But when personal income is unknown there is the added difficulty that the rate of taxation cannot be set. Those people whose sole income is salary or wages can be taxed easily at the source. The taxpayer must still make his final return; then the government can set its rate of taxation; then adjustments will have to be made.

The Budget-Mr. Castleden
I would offer this criticism, that the tax structure is becoming much too involved and will need simplification. Also the machinery of collection is far too complicated ; it is leading to the setting up of a bureaucracy. When we remember that we have to pay in 1943 the remainder of the eight months of 1942 tax, in addition to the 1943 taxes, there will be some very severe cuts in family incomes. The worker will have extremely little left with which to purchase consumer goods. The people of Canada are asked to buy bonds, to buy until it hurts: billions of dollars will be required. Before these people will go out and buy bonds they will want to know two or three things. One of the most important is, that the money which the government is spending is being spent profitably, without waste. That is why I think the government would have been well advised to investigate all charges of waste, subterfuge and downright trickery, according to an alleged report a short time ago.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What are they?

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The charges of
Colonel Thompson, I understand.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
He has
resigned.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Another thing of which they should be assured is that what happened to bonds after the last war will not be permitted to happen after the present one. I remember that, upon returning to civil life after the last war, I purchased a few small bonds. In later years, when the depression came and I needed a little money, I went to the bank to sell them. The banker said, "No, we do not buy bonds." I asked, "Where can I sell them? What good are they?" He said he thought he knew where I could sell them. I went round the corner and up a flight of stairs, and there the man ini charge of one of our free enterprise businesses said he would give me about ninety-two cents on the dollar. We should guard against a recurrence of this kind of thing.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Those were not Dominion of Canada bonds?

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
These were victory
bonds of the last war.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
And the bank did not take
them?

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
No, the bank did not take them.
Canada's expenditures in 1942-43 chargeable to war appropriations will amount, according
to the Minister of Finance, to the grand total of $4,558,000,000. Against that the government expects to raise in the fiscal year $2,218,000,000, leaving a balance to 'be borrowed, in the form of war loans, victory bonds and certificates, et cetera, of over $2,250,000,000. This amount will be added to the national debt, and interest on that debt must be paid. The debt is climbing rapidly. The minister himself estimated the national debt of Canada as of March 31, 1943, at $6,306,779,000. It has doubled since the war began. It has multiplied over twenty times in the last thirty years. The future of Canada is being mortgaged at an alarming rate. The workers, the soldiers, those engaged in war to-day are bearing the brunt of this battle; the great masses of the Canadian people are paying, and paying nobly, the heaviest tax which was ever placed upon the backs of the Canadian people. This year alone we are expected to pay approximately $500,000,000 more than the total cost of the war of 1914-18 and rehabilitation activities after that war; but in spite of that we are paying less than half of this year's expenditure on the war. Truly the world is learning that war is an expensive business, and unfortunately for the masses of the people everywhere war is a Business with a big "B." It is the people who have least to do with, the causing of these wars who must do most of the suffering and the paying.
One fact with regard to money which I think everyone should realize is that, even though spent in war, it is not actually lost. When a shell costing $1,000 is fired into the air it does not mean that with the firing of the shell the money it cost is destroyed. When a $2,000,000 warship sinks in the Atlantic, it does not mean that $2,000,000 worth of cash money goes to the bottom of the sea. It is not entirely lost. Either it is in circulation or stored away in deposits of one kind or another. When we eat food we do not destroy the money which was spent to buy it. In contracting for war equipment, money goes to the contractor, who pays it out in labour, in payments to those who supply him with steel and other materials, and for transportation; he sets aside certain reserves, and he distributes the profits among the shareholders of the company. About $5,500,000,000 was spent last year in Canada. Most of that money is still in the country. Its circulation has resulted in one of the greatest industrial booms Canada has ever known. People's incomes have increased, and in- spite of some of the heaviest taxation ever imposed, industry is still piling up profits. It would be foolish for anyone to deny that
The Budget-Mr. Castleden

business is profiting, and profiting largely, out of this war. There are big accumulations of wealth in Canada. Some of them are greater' as a result of the war.
But it ought to be remembered, along with that situation, that many families in Canada now have lost, and in future many more, if this war continues, will lose, fathers, brothers and sons. In view of the sacrifices which are being made of life and limb, nobody dares try to justify the amassing and hoarding of wealth through war. We of this group have continued to advocate that the government should levy non-interest bearing loans against these pools of wealth. If that were done, there would be no need of burdening future generations with a load of debt. If what happened after the last war happens again, in countries burdened with heavy national debts people will be denied a good living in order that they shall pay interest. According to the present set-up interest comes first, before food and clothing, before shoes for the children, before medical treatment for those who need it. In borrowing money, as we have done, to pay interest on our debt, we are doing nothing more than changing ordinary interest into compound interest. That, if it continues, is bound- to pyramid to ultimate and inevitable collapse. It simply cannot continue. There must be some fundamental change in our whole financial set-up. I have heard advocated in the house that we must remember that we owe this debt to ourselves, that we owe it to Canada. We owe it to ourselves, yes, just like the mortgage on the farm. Some group of officials of the Canada Permanent Mortgage Corporation-a-nd "permanent" is a good name- sitting in Toronto, own the mortgage. But we are not any better off on the farm because we owe the mortgage. We still have to go without the necessities of life in order to pay the interest on that mortgage.
Some so-called good Canadians have been reaping the fruits of the labour of the masses. If governments in Canada persist in thinking in these pre-war terms, we are going to fail. To return to an outmoded economy of the thirties will be a return to the bread-lines for the soldiers and sailors, the men- and women who return from the war. We shall have unemployment, want and poverty again.
A great deal was said in this chamber recently about free enterprise. I think the term ought to be clarified. During those disastrous thirties, what was called free enterprise? It was the right of monopolies to carry on their exploitation, the right of people to

form monopolies, the right of people to control complete industries, the right of people to control the credit and currency of the nation. That is what brought the world to chaos and to war. It brought people in Canada to poverty and need, and we sank into almost hopeless poverty.
I would point out to lion, members who are using the terms "free enterprise" and "private initiative" that the distress of the thirties did more to destroy individual initiative among the masses of the people than any other thing I know of.
We in the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation have for our objective the making of a society in Canada which will develop the initiative of the people, bring out the fullest expression of their talents and abilities. Nothing has done more to destroy this process than this so-called free enterprise in Canada. What we mean by free enterprise is the development of that initiative in individuals which has been crushed. What these other people are talking about when they refer to free enterprise is the right to create monopolies, the right to control, the right of privileged groups to have the power to work their will freely on. the Canadian economy. It is quite clear to-day that many groups who have had that privilege in the past are doing their best to see to it that that power and privilege will be maintained in the post-war period. There must be fundamental changes, deep changes. There must be a different outlook.
I do not like to hear people using the term "free enterprise" when they mean almost the opposite. The Cooperative Commonwealth Federation amendment to the budget calls for the nationalization of the whole banking system of Canada.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Would the hon. member give his definition of free enterprise?

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The right of the masses of the people, the right of everyone, to develop his own talents, abilities, and initiative. We want to see him have the right to own and develop those things around himself, but without the power to exploit his neighbour.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: And does that mean compulsory interest-free loans?

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is an entirely different matter. We have advocated compulsory interest-free loans under our present system.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Let them define private enterprise; they are advocating it.

The Budget-Mr. Castleden

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The Cooperative Commonwealth Federation amendment calls for the nationalization of banks in Canada. The purpose is, first, to make a more effective war effort now; second, to prevent a large interest bearing debt from being placed upon the people after the war and, third, to lay the foundation for the rebuilding of a new Canadian society.
What have we in the organization of the banks, as we have them to-day? Why can we not leave the banks as they are? If we look over the organization of some of the banks we find some interesting things. We soon find out why it is they wish to maintain control over the currency and credit of the nation. The chartered banks constitute one of the bulwarks through which monopolistic enterprise works. They keep competition out of their own privileged fields, and maintain control.
I should like to place on record to-night the names of some of the companies in which some of the directors of three of our more important banks in Canada act as directors. I shall turn first to the Canadian Bank of Commerce, and I find that one of the directors is president of Dominion Securities Corporation Limited, Brompton Pulp and Paper Company Limited, St. Lawrence Paper Mills Limited, Debentures Securities, Confederation Life, Toronto Mortgage Company, General Shareholding Corporation Limited, and six other finance companies.
Another director is president of Sawyer-Massey Limited, president of Western Canada Flour Mills, and a director of Asbestos Corporation, the Hamilton Bridge Company, St. Lawrence Corporation and Brompton Pulp and Paper Company. This gentleman is also the oil controller of Canada.
Another director is chairman of the largest export company in British Columbia. He is chairman of British Columbia Packers, and is interested in British Columbia Plywoods and at least twelve other companies. He is director of International Nickel Company, of which I shall have more to say later, and a director of Western Trust, British Columbia Power Company, and Forest Investment Company.
Another director is president of Canada Packers and is also a director of British Columbia Packers.
Another director is a director of the Imperial Life Insurance Company, and is vice-president and director of the National Trust Company.
Then, turning to the Bank of Montreal, we find that one of its directors is president of the Royal Trust Company, and a director of the Canada and Dominion Sugar Company.
Another director of the Bank of Montreal was, a year or two ago, president of the Canadian Pacific Railway, Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company, West Kootenay Power Company and Canadian Airways. He was also a director of the Royal Trust Company, the Sun Life Assurance Company, the Royal Exchange, the Waldorf-Astoria hotel, Canadian Industries Limited, and Canadian Investment Fund.
Another director was president of the Cock-shutt Plow Company, and a director of Frost and Wood, Gypsum Lime and Alabastine Canada Limited, Bell Telephone Company, International Nickel Company of Canada, and on the advisory board of the Sun Life Assurance Company.
Another director is president of the Bell Telephone Company and the North American Telegraph Company. He is also a director of Northern Electric, the Royal Trust Company, Mutual Life Assurance Company, Consolidated Paper Corporation, Liverpool and Globe Insurance Company, Globe Indemnity Company and others.
Another director is director of the Mutual Life Assurance Company, the Bell Telephone Company, the Steel Company of Canada, the Royal Trust Company, Dominion Glass, and he, like the hon. member who preceded me, was interested, because he is a director of Borden's Limited and John Labatt Limited, in the beverages people drink, from the cradle to the grave.
Then we come to the Royal Bank of Canada and we find some very interesting directors. One is vice-president and executive manager of the Montreal Trust, director of Canadian Airways, of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, the Sun Life Assurance Company and Ogilvie Flour Mills.
Another director is chairman of the Dominion Bridge Company, the Dominion Engineering Works, and a director of the Steel Company of Canada, Shawinigan Water and Power Company, Fairchild Aircraft, Montreal Trust, Consumers Cordage, and Canadian Pratt and Whitney Aircraft.
Another director is president of the Northern Electric Company, Amalgamated Electric, Canadian Associated Aircraft Limited; and a director of the Montreal Trust Company, Belding-Corticelli Limited, Lake of the Woods Milling Company, the Bell Telephone Company, Dominion Engineering Works, Dominion Bridge Company, Shawinigan Water and Power Company and others.
Another director of the Royal Bank used to sit with the party to my right in this house.
The Budget-Mr. Castleden

He was also a director of E. B. Eddy Company. He has now, I believe, gone to the House of Lords in England.
Another director was president of the Howard Smith Paper Mills, Canada Paper, Alliance Paper, Allied War Supplies Corporation, director of Montreal Trust Company, Adams Paper and Canadian Chamber of Commerce.
Another director was president and managing director of Dominion Bridge, president of Dominion Engineering Works, vice-president and director of Canadian Car and Foundry Company, director of Bell Telephone Company, Canadian Locomotive, Northern Electric, Montreal Trust, Montreal Light, Heat and Power Consolidated, and, oddly enough, of Beauharnois Light, Heat and Power Company.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

speechtext: Name one member who has spoken who gave that as a definition.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You can make your own speech afterwards.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The hon. member wants to keep the present system, does he not? And that is the present system.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Name one member who has spoken up to the present time who gave that group as representing private enterprise.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Those speaking of private enterprise are constantly saying that private enterprise must be maintained in this country. This is what you have under your private enterprise. This is the root cause why the Liberal promises made in the 1919 convention cannot be fulfilled. Two things are seen pretty clearly: one, that the Canadian people will never know economic security, never be free from want and fear until the banks of Canada, the financial system of Canada, can be nationalized. That is why we call for it in this resolution. Two, the supply of new productive equipment to work on the nationalized resources of this country to supply the needs of the people of Canada can never take place under the present set-up, while the present privileged groups control our currency and1 finance and, through that, control the industries. A national banking system with its head at the Bank of Canada would be the proper means of nationalizing the financing of Canada. It then could control the price levels and regulate foreign exchange operations. That is one of the first essentials to social security. It was the first step that the farmer-labour government of New Zealand found necessary before they could institute any real reform within that nation.
I should like to place on record an example of how one of the largest monopolistic corporations of the world receives special considerations from this government. I maintain that this is not warranted when Canada is passing through a crisis such as that of to-day.
In August, 1941, a special agreement was entered into between His Majesty the King in the right of Canada and the International Nickel Company of Canada Limited.
